```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 5.6, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Experience sampling studies ask participants to report their current state
several times a day over days or weeks. The resulting data answer questions
that a single questionnaire cannot: whether emotions change over the course of
a study, whether some days differ from others, and whether the time of day
matters. They also raise a presentation problem. Averaging each day to one
number hides how the responses are distributed, and a separate histogram for
each day spreads the comparison over many panels. A snake plot of the daily
distributions keeps one band per day in study order, so the distribution of
every day and its change from one day to the next are read in one figure.

This case study analyses the anger and happiness ratings of a cohort of
university students over 14 study days. It first establishes the structure of
the study (which days, how many answers), then asks whether the share of
high-anger answers changes over the study, whether happiness differs between
weekdays and weekends, and when in the day the answers are given. Each question
is answered first with numbers computed from the data and then with
`survey_snake()` in its experience sampling mode (`var`, `day`,
`timestamp`).

```{r package}
library(snakeplot)
```

## Data

`ema_beeps` holds every answered prompt ("beep") of the experience sampling
study of Neubauer and Schmiedek (2024; data CC-BY 4.0 at
<https://osf.io/bhq3p>). Each row is one beep.

- **Participant:** `id` — anonymised identifier; beeps are nested within
  participants.
- **Study day:** `day` — 1 to 14; one band per day in the plots.
- **Time stamp:** `start_time` — date and clock time of the beep.
- **Happiness:** `happy` — 1 (not at all) to 5 (extremely), rescaled from
  the original 1–7.
- **Anger:** `angry` — 1 (not at all) to 5 (extremely), rescaled from the
  original 1–7.

```{r data}
with(ema_beeps, c(beeps = length(id), participants = length(unique(id))))
scale_labels <- c("1" = "Not at all", "2" = "Slightly", "3" = "Moderately",
                  "4" = "Quite", "5" = "Extremely")
```

The data hold 11,474 beeps from 321 participants. `scale_labels` maps the
five levels to the labels shown in the legends.

## The structure of the study

Before comparing days, it is necessary to know what a study day is. The first
question is on which weekday each study day falls.

```{r weekdays}
with(ema_beeps, table(day, weekday = format(start_time, "%a")))
```

Every study day falls on one weekday for all participants: days 1 to 7 run
from Monday to Sunday, and days 8 to 14 again from Monday to Sunday. The next
question is whether days 7 and 8 are consecutive. For each participant who
answered on both days, the number of calendar days between them is computed.

```{r burst-gap}
burst_gap <- aggregate(cbind(gap = as.numeric(as.Date(start_time))) ~ id,
                       data = subset(ema_beeps, day %in% c(7, 8)),
                       FUN = \(x) diff(range(x)))
with(subset(burst_gap, gap > 0), table(days_between_day7_and_day8 = gap))
```

For all 209 participants who answered on both days, day 8 comes 43 days after
day 7. The study therefore consists of two measurement weeks, each running
from Monday to Sunday, six weeks apart. Day 8 is the first day of the second
week, not the day after day 7, and any change between days 7 and 8 may
reflect the six weeks in between.

The third question is how many participants and beeps contribute to each day.

```{r per-day}
merge(aggregate(id ~ day, data = ema_beeps, FUN = \(x) length(unique(x))),
      aggregate(cbind(beeps = happy) ~ day, data = ema_beeps, FUN = length))
```

The number of participants falls from 304 on day 1 to 175 on day 14, and the
number of beeps from 1,161 to 536. Within each week, participation declines
from Monday to Sunday (304 to 234 participants in the first week, 240 to 175
in the second). Every daily distribution below is therefore based on a
different, shrinking set of participants, and a change in the distribution
can come from a change in emotions or from a change in who answers.

## Does the share of high-anger beeps change?

Anger is rare in these data, so the question is about the upper part of the
scale: does the share of beeps with anger rated *moderately* or higher change
over the study? The full distribution of anger per day, in percent of that
day's beeps:

```{r anger-table}
round(100 * prop.table(xtabs(~ day + angry, data = ema_beeps), margin = 1), 1)
```

On every day, between 72.5% and 82.9% of the beeps report no anger at all.
The share of beeps at levels 3 to 5 is the sum of the last three columns; it
is computed per day and per week below.

```{r anger-high}
anger <- transform(ema_beeps,
                   high_anger = angry >= 3,
                   week = ifelse(day <= 7, "first", "second"))
aggregate(high_anger ~ day, data = anger, FUN = mean)
aggregate(high_anger ~ week, data = anger, FUN = mean)
```

The share of high-anger beeps lies between 4.6% (day 7) and 8.9% (day 1) in
the first week and between 6.9% (day 13) and 9.6% (day 11) in the second. Over
the whole week it rises from 7.1% to 8.3%, a difference of 1.2 percentage
points. The largest single change is from day 7 to day 8, where the share of
beeps with no anger falls from 81.5% to 72.5% and the share at level 2 rises
from 13.9% to 19.2%.

Because each participant contributes several beeps, days on which a few
participants answer often weigh those participants heavily. Averaging within
participants first, and then across participants, gives every participant the
same weight:

```{r anger-person}
person_day <- aggregate(angry ~ id + day, data = ema_beeps, FUN = mean)
merge(aggregate(cbind(beep_mean = angry) ~ day, data = ema_beeps, FUN = mean),
      aggregate(cbind(person_mean = angry) ~ day, data = person_day, FUN = mean))
```

The two means differ by at most 0.04 on any day (1.36 against 1.40 on day 1),
and both are highest on day 8 (1.43). The rise at the start of the second week
is therefore not an artefact of a few participants answering many beeps. The
analysis is descriptive; it does not test whether the day-to-day differences
exceed what the sampling of participants would produce.

The stacked bars draw the percentage table above, one band per day:

```{r anger-bars}
survey_snake(ema_beeps, var = "angry", day = "day", tick_shape = "bar",
             colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5),
             level_labels = scale_labels, title = "Anger by study day")
```

Each band is one study day, divided into segments whose widths are the
percentages of the day's beeps at each level, from *not at all* on the left;
the percentage is written in each segment wide enough to hold it. The diamond
marks the day's mean rating and the band is shaded by that mean. The
comparison of interest, the share in the three right-hand segments, is small
on every day, which matches the 4.6% to 9.6% computed above; the widest
change between neighbouring bands is the drop of the left-hand segment from
day 7 to day 8.

## Are the weekends happier?

Happiness is common rather than rare: most beeps are rated *quite* happy. The
question is whether the share of the highest rating differs between weekdays
and weekends, which the weekday table above locates on days 6, 7, 13 and 14.

```{r happy-table}
round(100 * prop.table(xtabs(~ day + happy, data = ema_beeps), margin = 1), 1)
aggregate(happy ~ weekend,
          data = transform(ema_beeps, weekend = day %in% c(6, 7, 13, 14)),
          FUN = mean)
```

The share of beeps rated *extremely* happy rises within each week: from 9.1%
on Monday (day 1) to 19.2% on Sunday (day 7) in the first week, and from 12.0%
(day 8) to 16.2% (day 14) in the second. The mean happiness is 3.67 on
weekend days and 3.50 on weekdays. The share at level 4 is close to half on
every day (46.8% to 54.2%), so the weekly change takes place in the upper
tail.

The tick version of the plot draws every beep rather than every percentage.
Each tick is one beep; the ticks of each level occupy a zone whose width is
that level's share of the day's beeps. `bar_reverse` is not needed here
because the zones run from level 1 on the left to level 5 on the right.

```{r happy-ticks}
survey_snake(ema_beeps, var = "happy", day = "day",
             colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5),
             level_labels = scale_labels, title = "Happiness by study day")
```

The bars show the same comparison as exact percentages. With
`bar_reverse = TRUE` the segments start from *extremely* on the left, so the
segment that changes within each week, the share of *extremely*, starts at
the same position in every band and its widths can be compared directly.

```{r happy-bars}
survey_snake(ema_beeps, var = "happy", day = "day", tick_shape = "bar",
             bar_reverse = TRUE, colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5),
             level_labels = scale_labels, title = "Happiness by study day")
```

Ticks keep the number of beeps visible (day 1 has 1,161 ticks, day 14 has
536), while bars give the shares a reader can compare against the table. For
the question asked here, a change in one segment, the bars with the segment
aligned at the left edge are the more precise display.

## When in the day are beeps answered?

The last question concerns the clock rather than the calendar. The number of
beeps per hour of the day, and the mean ratings in each hour:

```{r hours}
timing <- transform(ema_beeps, hour = format(start_time, "%H"))
with(timing, table(hour))
aggregate(cbind(happy, angry) ~ hour, data = timing, FUN = mean)
```

All beeps are answered between 07:00 and 17:59, with between 979 and 1,291
beeps in each hour from 7 to 16 and 111 in the hour from 17:00. Mean
happiness rises from 3.45 in the hour from 7:00 to 3.61 in the hour from
16:00 (3.63 from 17:00, based on 111 beeps); mean anger stays between 1.30
and 1.38 in every hour. Happiness is higher later in the day; anger does not
follow the clock.

With `timestamp`, `survey_snake()` places each tick at its clock time instead
of in a level zone, and colours it by the response level. The band then
spans the full 24 hours, with guides at 6h, 12h and 18h. The mean marker is
switched off because its horizontal position encodes the mean rating, which
has no meaning on a time axis.

```{r happy-clock}
survey_snake(ema_beeps, var = "happy", day = "day", timestamp = "start_time",
             show_mean = FALSE, colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5),
             level_labels = scale_labels,
             title = "Happiness by study day and time of day")
```

Each tick is one beep, at the time it was answered and in the colour of its
happiness rating. All ticks fall between the 6h and 18h guides, which is the
07:00 to 17:59 window computed above; the beeps of every day are spread over
that window rather than concentrated at a few times.

## Conclusions

- The 14 study days are two Monday-to-Sunday weeks, six weeks (43 days)
  apart. Day-to-day comparisons across day 7 and day 8 span that gap.
- Participation falls from 304 participants on day 1 to 175 on day 14, and
  falls within each week.
- Anger is absent in 72.5% to 82.9% of the beeps on every day. The share of
  beeps at *moderately* angry or above rises from 7.1% in the first week to
  8.3% in the second, and mean anger is highest on day 8, the first day of the
  second week, whether beeps or participants are weighted equally.
- The share of *extremely* happy beeps rises from Monday to Sunday in both
  weeks; mean happiness is 3.67 on weekend days and 3.50 on weekdays.
- Happiness rises slightly over the day (3.45 at 7:00 to 3.61 at 16:00);
  anger does not change with the time of day.
- Stacked bars (`tick_shape = "bar"`) give the exact daily shares; ticks keep
  the number of beeps visible; `timestamp` positions every beep on the clock.

The same data can also be drawn as a sequence or as clock-time activity; see
[the sequences guide](sequences.html) and [the activity guide](activity.html).

## Reference

Neubauer, A. B., & Schmiedek, F. (2024). Approaching academic adjustment on
multiple time scales. *Zeitschrift für Erziehungswissenschaft, 27*(1),
147–168. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11618-023-01182-8>
